{{Short description|Rotation of a circle by an angle of π times an irrational number}}

[[File:Sturmian-sequence-from-irrational-rotation.gif|thumb|right|Sturmian sequence generated by irrational rotation with theta=0.2882748715208621 and x=0.078943143]]

An '''irrational rotation''' in the mathematical theory of [[dynamical system]]s, is defined as a [[Map (mathematics)|map]] <math>f</math>, as follows:

Let <math>x\in [0, 1)</math> be arbitrary, and let <math>\theta</math> be any irrational number. For  <math>i\in</math> {{math |1={{mset|0, 1, 2 ...}} }} define<ref name="Dynamical Systems on the Circle">{{Cite web |last=Turer |first=George |title=Dynamical Systems on the Circle |url=https://math.uchicago.edu/~may/REU2019/REUPapers/Turer.pdf |access-date=August 11, 2026 |website=Math Department, University of Chicago}}</ref> <math>f^i_\theta : [0,1) \rightarrow [0,1)</math> by
:<math>f^i_\theta(x) = x + i\cdot\theta</math>  (mod 1)

Under the identification of a [[circle]] with {{math|'''R'''/'''Z'''}}, or with the interval {{math|[0, 1)}} with the boundary points glued together, this map becomes a [[rotation]] of a [[circle]] by a proportion {{math|''&theta;''}} of a full revolution (i.e., an angle of {{math|2''&pi;&theta;''}}&nbsp;radians). Since {{math|''&theta;''}} is irrational, the rotation has infinite [[Order (group theory)|order]] in the [[circle group]], and the map {{math|''f''<sub>''&theta;''</sub>}} has no [[periodic orbit]]s.

Alternatively, we can use multiplicative notation for an irrational rotation by introducing the map
: <math> f_\theta :S^1 \to S^1, \quad \quad \quad f_\theta(x)=xe^{2\pi i\theta} </math>

The relationship between the additive and multiplicative notations is the group isomorphism
:<math> \varphi:([0,1),+) \to (S^1, \cdot) \quad \varphi(x)=xe^{2\pi i\theta}</math>.

It can be shown that {{math|''&phi;''}} is an [[isometry]].

There is a strong distinction in circle rotations that depends on whether {{math|''&theta;''}} is rational or irrational. Rational rotations are less interesting examples of dynamical systems because if <math>\theta = \frac{a}{b}</math> and <math>\gcd(a,b) = 1</math>, then <math>f_\theta^b(x) = x</math> when <math>x \isin [0,1)</math>.  It can also be shown that 
<math>f_\theta^i(x) \ne x</math> when <math>1 \le i < b</math>.

== Significance ==
Irrational rotations form a fundamental example in the theory of [[dynamical system]]s. According to the [[Denjoy's theorem on rotation number|Denjoy theorem]], every orientation-preserving {{math|''C''<sup>2</sup>}}-diffeomorphism of the circle with an irrational [[rotation number]] {{math|''&theta;''}} is [[topologically conjugate]] to {{math|''f''<sub>''&theta;''</sub>}}. An irrational rotation is a [[measure-preserving transformation|measure-preserving]] [[ergodic transformation]], but it is not [[mixing (physics)|mixing]]. The [[Poincaré map]] for the dynamical system associated with the [[Foliation#Linear_and_Kronecker_foliations|Kronecker foliation]] on a [[torus]] with angle {{math|''&theta;''>}} is the irrational rotation by {{math|''&theta;''}}. [[C*-algebra]]s associated with irrational rotations, known as [[noncommutative torus|irrational rotation algebras]], have been extensively studied.

== Properties ==
* If {{math|''&theta;''}} is irrational, then the orbit of any element of {{math|[0, 1]}} under the rotation {{math|''f''<sub>''&theta;''</sub>}} is [[Dense set|dense]] in {{math|[0, 1)}}. Therefore, irrational rotations are [[topologically transitive]].
* Irrational (and rational) rotations are not [[topologically mixing]].
* Irrational rotations are uniquely [[ergodicity|ergodic]], with the Lebesgue measure serving as the unique invariant probability measure.
* Suppose {{math|[''a'', ''b''] &sub; [0, 1)}}. Since {{math|''f''<sub>''&theta;''</sub>}} is ergodic,<br/><math> \text{lim} _ {N \to \infty} \frac{1}{N} \sum_{n=0}^{N-1} \chi_{[a,b)}(f_\theta ^n (t))=b-a </math>.

==Generalizations==
* Circle rotations are examples of [[Translation (group theory)|group translations]].
* For a general orientation preserving homomorphism {{math|''f''}} of {{math|''S''<sup>1</sup>}} to itself we call a homeomorphism <math> F:\mathbb{R}\to \mathbb{R} </math> a ''lift'' of {{math|''f''}} if <math> \pi \circ F=f \circ \pi </math> where <math> \pi (t)=t \bmod 1 </math>.<ref name=Fisher/>
* The circle rotation can be thought of as a subdivision of a circle into two parts, which are then exchanged with each other. A subdivision into more than two parts, which are then permuted with one-another, is called an [[interval exchange transformation]].
* Rigid rotations of [[compact group]]s effectively behave like circle rotations; the invariant measure is the [[Haar measure]].

==Applications==
* Skew Products over Rotations of the Circle: In 1969<ref name=Veech/> [[William A. Veech]] constructed examples of [[minimal (mathematics)|minimal]] and not uniquely ergodic dynamical systems as follows: "Take two copies of the unit circle and mark off segment {{math|''J''}} of length {{math|2''&pi;&alpha;''}} in the counterclockwise direction on each one with endpoint at 0. Now take {{math|''&theta;''}} irrational and consider the following dynamical system. Start with a point {{math|''p''}}, say in the first circle. Rotate counterclockwise by {{math|2''&pi;&theta;''}} until the first time the orbit lands in {{math|''J''}}; then switch to the corresponding point in the second circle, rotate by {{math|2''&pi;&theta;''}} until the first time the point lands in {{math|''J''}}; switch back to the first circle and so forth. Veech showed that if {{math|''&theta;''}} is irrational, then there exists irrational {{math|''&alpha;''}} for which this system is minimal and the [[Lebesgue measure]] is not uniquely ergodic."<ref name=Masur/>
